sources.title: How should I care for my Siamese fighting fish?
Care and Use of Siamese Fighting Fish (Betta splendens) for Research
Betta Fish Fin Rot: Symptoms, Causes, and Treatment
Ép cá Betta trong điều kiện nguồn thức ăn hạn chế (Made In 2 Lúa)

facts.fact: Wild Betta splendens is native to central Thailand. Seriously Fish says records from Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia and the Mekong basin refer to other species or to introduced populations.
In the wild it lives in still or slow water such as rice paddies, swamps, ditches and ponds, often shaded and sometimes low in dissolved oxygen.
Maximum size is 70 mm SL.
Lifespan is about 2 years under laboratory conditions.
Ornamental strains are more aggressive than other Betta species. Cheap mass-produced veiltails may carry genetic defects.
Tank size: 20 L or more is ideal and 10 L is the absolute minimum. A community tank needs at least 40 L.
A tank with a 45 × 30 cm base (about 41 L) suits one male or a pair.
Use at least a 5-gallon glass or plastic tank. Bettas should not live in bowls.
Use a lid, because bettas jump, and leave air space between the water and the lid.
Keep the water at 24–26°C with a submersible heater. RSPCA Australia says room temperature is generally too cold and fluctuates.
Seriously Fish gives a temperature range of 22–30 °C, pH 6.0–8.0 (wild fish likely prefer 5.0–7.0) and hardness of 1–15 dGH.
Keep the water at 76°F to 81°F with an in-tank heater and check it with a thermometer.
Targets: ammonia below 0.1 ppm, nitrite below 0.2 ppm, nitrate below 50 ppm and pH 6.5–7.5.
In a new tank, test ammonia and nitrite every 2–3 days for the first six weeks, then every 1–2 weeks.
Use a filter with adjustable flow, since bettas prefer low flow. Add an air stone if the surface is not stirred.
Change 10–25% of the water each week and clean the gravel.
Rinse the filter in tank water, not tap water, because chlorine can kill beneficial bacteria.
Keep the lights on for no more than 10 hours a day, with at least 8 hours of darkness, and keep the tank out of direct sunlight.
Provide plants or other cover.
Feed once a day, only what is eaten in under two minutes. Use betta pellets or granules, with occasional frozen black worms, brine shrimp, tubifex or daphnia.
Feed pellets or flakes daily, an amount eaten within 3 to 5 minutes, and give bloodworms or brine shrimp treats in moderation.
Captive bettas accept dried food but need regular live or frozen foods such as Daphnia, Artemia and bloodworm.
In a laboratory, adults were fed newly hatched brine shrimp once a day plus pellets once a day (about 10 Golden Pearls of 500–800 µm, or 2–3 Ken's 1-mm pellets).
In a laboratory, mating success fell to about 30% on diets of dried food only.
Breeding: bettas build bubble nests. Eggs hatch in 24–48 hours and the fry stay in the nest for 3–4 more days while the male guards them.
Give the female plenty of cover when breeding. The pair need not be separated before spawning.
Feed fry infusoria for the first few days, then microworm and Artemia nauplii. Some reports link too much Artemia to health problems in young bettas.
In a laboratory, larvae were not fed until 5 days after fertilisation, then got rotifers. From day 15 they got newly hatched brine shrimp 2–4 times daily.
In a laboratory, females needed at least 4 weeks between matings and males about 1 week. Fish matured around 10 weeks.
Interfish Thailand's egg tofu food can be fed to bettas from 3 weeks old.

A Vietnamese keeper (hhhnam) reports breeding bettas in a styrofoam box of about 40×60×40 cm. It had 3–5 cm of clay soil mixed with chopped grass and water spinach, and was left about a week to clear and grow natural food.
The same keeper reports the fry ate only natural food for about the first 10 days. After that they got 'con mẻ' microworms cultured on cold rice, and later chopped tubifex (trùn chỉ).
The same keeper removes the female after spawning and the male about 3–4 days after the fry hatch.
Never keep two males together. Keep males and females together only for breeding.
Bettas kept with other bettas fight and can die.
Snails or large shrimp can be suitable tankmates, but smaller shrimp may be eaten.
Corydoras, otocinclus and neon tetras (in a shoal of five or more) may be suitable tankmates. Widow, serape and cochu blue tetras are not recommended because they nip fins.
Keep a backup tank ready in case of aggression or fin nipping.
Snails, ghost shrimp, certain fish and African dwarf frogs can be tankmates, but they need a larger tank and better filtration.
Bettas are not recommended for standard community tanks. Avoid tankmates with trailing fins or looks that a male may take for a rival.
Signs of poor health: sinking, or bobbing at the surface, lumps, wounds, clamped fins, trailing faeces, and staying in a corner for long periods.
Fin rot signs: ragged or shortened fins, brown, red, black or white edges, white fuzz or a mucus-like film, clamped fins, hiding and poor appetite.
Fin rot causes include poor water quality (ammonia, high nitrate), temperature swings or cool water, injuries from sharp decor or nippy tankmates, overcrowding, stress and poor nutrition.
Chlorine, chloramine and heavy metals in tap water can cause immunosuppression or serious illness.
Velvet in bettas is caused by Oodinium, a dinoflagellate.
Ammonia is harmful above 0.25 ppm.
A fish that keeps hiding or is lethargic and unresponsive should get veterinary care.
For mild fin rot, make small water changes every two to three days, test the water and replace sharp decor.
For moderate fin rot, move the betta to a hospital tank and consider an antibacterial such as API Bettafix. Follow the label and your vet.
Remove activated carbon from the filter before medicating, because it can absorb the medicine.
In a laboratory, velvet was treated with Proform C at 30 µL/L for 5 days, with a 100% water change daily.
In a laboratory, mild fin rot was treated with nitrofurazone (Furan 2) at 46 mg/L for 4 days, with a 100% water change daily.
In a laboratory, methylene blue at 3 ppm for 5 days was used during quarantine and for injured mating fish.
About half of laboratory 'bloat' cases resolved after a 24- or 48-hour fast.
Treating mycobacteriosis in bettas has had minimal success.
Quarantine new fish or plants for at least two weeks.
In a laboratory, new fish were quarantined for at least 1 week, with 1 extra week for wild-caught fish.
Avoid overfeeding, because bettas are prone to obesity.
Sharp decorations can tear fins.
Avoid mammal fats such as beef heart, meat and offal.
Avoid mirrors, which make males flare constantly and cause stress.
The idea that bettas can live in bowls is wrong, says Veterinary Medicine at Illinois (quoting Dr. Krista Keller). Bowls are often too small for normal swimming and hiding.
